newsitem.title: INDIA: New Kashmir leader takes charge, promises normalcy.
newsitem.headline: New Kashmir leader takes charge, promises normalcy.

text.p: The leader of Kashmir's largest pro-India party took office on Wednesday at the head of the region's first local government since a separatist revolt broke out nearly seven years ago.

Under tight security, National Conference chairman Farooq Abdullah was sworn in as chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state in a ceremony in Srinagar, the state's summer capital and the focus of the separatist insurgency.
"We must turn trouble-torn Kashmir again into heaven," Abdullah, 59, said in a speech after the ceremony, during which he twice broke down in tears.
"For that I appeal to the people of India and Kashmir for their support. I warn Pakistan not to stick its leg into our business," he said, speaking in Urdu.
India accuses neighbouring Pakistan of arming guerrillas who seek independence or union with Pakistan. Pakistan says it only provides moral and diplomatic support.

Heavy-set Abdullah, dressed in a dark-coloured Nehru jacket and peaked lambs'-wool cap, smiled and hugged many of the 1,000-odd guests at the oath-taking ceremony in a large conference hall on picturesque Dal Lake.
Shops, businesses and schools in the Moslem-dominated Kashmir valley were closed after separatists opposed to the new government called for a strike throughout the Himalayan region.

Senior Indian politicians from a range of parties attended the ceremony, closing ranks with Abdullah despite political differences to present a united face for the state, the only Moslem majority province in predominantly Hindu India.
Former prime minister V.P. Singh and Congress party president Sitaram Kesri attended the oath-taking.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's government and its allies said they would back Abdullah's bid to win autonomy for Kashmir.

"Our government has completed its promise by conducting free and fair elections in the state," Information and Broadcasting Minister C. M. Ibrahim said after the ceremony. "Now the central (federal) government is ready to help."
"We assure you that our party will strengthen article 370," Congress chief Kesri said, referring to the section of the Indian constitution that ensures the state a special position.
Abdullah contested the polls on a promise of autonomy for the region, which includes Hindu-dominated Jammu, the predominantly Moslem Kashmir valley, and Buddhist Ladakh.
Two dozen ministers also took the oath with Abdullah. Their portfolios have not yet been announced.
Last week Abdullah's party won 58 seats in the 87-member assembly in the first state elections since 1987, winning an absolute majority in a humiliating defeat of rivals.
"Nobody has lost the elections," an ebullient Abdullah said before the ceremony. "It is the win of everybody who believes in democracy. Whoever participated in the process is a winner."
Dozens of separatist groups in the valley have rejected Abdullah's government. They boycotted the polls, calling them a mockery of Kashmiri aspirations.
Kashmir's leading separatist coalition, the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, a combination of about 30 political parties, asked Kashmiris to observe a "Black Day" on Wednesday.
Kashmiri analysts said Abdullah's first tasks were to reconcile the separatists and put the battered economy back on track.
Police and hospital sources say more than 20,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence since 1990.
